add_comment.description: Pin feedback to passages without changing them - for reviews and critique ("what's weak here", "check this draft"). Every point of the reply goes in this one call's `comments`, in document order: name the block each is about by its id as `block`, and quote `anchor` only for a few words inside that block it is about. The user sees each comment as a card that jumps to its passage, so keep your reply to a short overall summary.

comments.description: The points, one per passage (each word, when asked to gloss words), in document order

anchor.description: Only for a few words inside that block: those words, verbatim. Left out, the comment is about the whole block.

block.description: The id shown before the block the comment is about, like `k3f9` from `[#k3f9]`

comment.description: The feedback, in the user's language - specific and actionable

suggestion.description: Only when the fix is a concrete rewrite: the anchor (or, without one, the whole block) as it should read, in markdown. The user can apply it in one click; leave it out for points that need the writer's own judgment.

check_conventions.description: Check text against the document's writing conventions with a deterministic rules engine: punctuation and spacing (full-width marks in Chinese and Japanese, French no-break spaces, quotes, dashes, ellipses), numbers and dates, spelling lists, and consistency with the rest of the document, under the conventions profile in force (shown in the result). Pass `heading` or a line range for part of the document (default: all of it), or `text` to check a draft before you propose it. Returns findings grouped by rule with line numbers, the text, the fix and why. Use it to ground proofreading and convention fixes instead of guessing; it changes nothing.

heading.description: Heading text of the section to check (case-insensitive, partial match). Takes precedence over the line range.

strict.description: Also report style hints (long sentences, wordy phrases, passive voice...). Default false.

text.description: A draft (markdown) to check instead of the document, judged against the document's own conventions.

edit_file.description: Change part of a file in the folder: `old` must appear in it exactly once, verbatim (read_file it first), and becomes `new`. Several changes to one file are several calls. Not for the open document - propose_edit changes that.

new.description: What it becomes; empty deletes it

old.description: The text to replace, verbatim, enough of it to be unique

find_files.description: Find files in the project folder by name - text files, and PDF, Word, PowerPoint, spreadsheet, EPUB and RTF files (case-insensitive; every word must appear in the path, so "chapter 3" finds drafts/chapter-3.md). Markdown and plain-text documents come first. Leave `name` out to list every file, to see what reference material there is; then read_file.

name.description: Part of the file's name or path; left out, every file

find_files+images.description: Find files in the project folder by name - text files, PDF, Word, PowerPoint, spreadsheet, EPUB and RTF files, and images, marked "(image)" (case-insensitive; every word must appear in the path, so "chapter 3" finds drafts/chapter-3.md). Markdown and plain-text documents come first. Leave `name` out to list every file, to see what reference material there is - notes, other chapters, pictures; then read_file.

name.description: Part of the file's name or path; left out, every file

measure_text.description: Count text exactly for a length limit - never estimate a count yourself. Metrics: x_weighted (X, limit 280: URLs count 23, CJK characters and emoji 2), bluesky (300 graphemes and 3,000 bytes), threads (500), instagram (2,200, at most 5 hashtags), mastodon (500 by default), linkedin (3,000, fold near 140), wechat_title (32), wechat_digest (120), wechat_content, xhs_title (20), xhs_body (1,000), weibo, govuk_title (65), govuk_summary (160), zh_academic_title (25 字), and plain chars, words, cjk_chars, utf8_bytes. Without `metric` it returns the basic counts. Use it on the exact text before proposing anything that must fit a platform's limit, and give the count in your reply. Not for new text with a length the user asked for: propose that directly - propose_edit's result gives its size.

metric.description: What to count, and against which limit.

text.description: The exact text to count, as it will be posted or used.

propose_edit.description: Propose edits to the document. Each lands as the user set it - a revision they accept or reject, or written straight in (their message says so). Every edit of the reply goes in this one call's `edits`, one item per distinct edit, in document order. For each, pick the action that matches the intent: `replace` swaps `anchor` for `text`; `replace_selection` swaps the user's currently selected text (the <selected-text> block in their message; no `anchor` needed) for `text`; `insert_before`/`insert_after` add `text` around an untouched `anchor` - inside the paragraph when the anchor is a phrase or sentence within it (write `text` as words that read on from it - after a paragraph's last sentence, this continues the paragraph), as a new paragraph when the anchor is a whole block or `text` is block content (a heading, list, several paragraphs), and as a new line of the same table or list when the anchor is a whole row or list item line and `text` is another one; `delete` removes `anchor`; `append` adds `text` at the end of the document; `insert_at_cursor` adds `text` exactly where the user's cursor is (only when their message carries a <cursor> block showing it; no `anchor` needed). Name the target by its block: every block of the document (a paragraph, a heading, a whole list, a quote, a table, a code block, a picture) starts with its id, like `[#k3f9]`, and `block` takes that id - write it first, before anything else, so the user sees where the edit goes at once. With `block` alone, `replace` swaps the whole block for `text`, `delete` removes it, and `insert_before`/`insert_after` add `text` as a new block next to it. To change a few words inside a block, give `block` and, as `anchor`, just those words quoted from it - not the whole block; to add text inside a block (after a sentence, or a list item of a list), give `block` and, as `anchor`, the words or the item line it goes next to. To rewrite a run of consecutive blocks in one replace - however long: a section, the whole document - give the first as `block` and the last as `last_block`, and the run rewritten as `text`. The user still decides on each paragraph by itself. Pictures in the run stay as they are, written in `text` as they were: a text edit never changes or removes a picture. When the user asks for a picture to change too (its people, its scene, its style), redo it with generate_image by its block first, then propose the text, in the same reply - writing that you changed it is not changing it. `delete` by its block removes one. The ids aren't part of the text: never write them in `text` or `anchor`. Words quoted in `anchor` must occur exactly once in the block - quote a few more if they repeat. Without `block` is only for text you proposed earlier that the user hasn't decided on, which has no id: then `anchor` quotes it verbatim, once.

edits.description: Every edit of this reply, in document order

action.description: What kind of edit this is

anchor.description: With `block`: only the few words inside that block the edit changes, quoted verbatim, once in the block - leave it out to change the whole block. Without `block` (only text you proposed that the user hasn't decided on): that text, quoted verbatim.

block.description: The id of the block the edit targets, as the document shows it before the block (`k3f9` for `[#k3f9]`). Write it first.

last_block.description: Only to rewrite a run of consecutive blocks in one replace: the id of the last of them, `block` being the first; `text` is then the run rewritten.

reason.description: One short sentence, in the language of your reply, on why this change - shown on the proposal card so the user can judge it at a glance (e.g. "Cut the repeated point about cost").

text.description: The new content (markdown). Required for every action except `delete`.

read_document.description: Read part of the document verbatim: a whole section by its heading (subsections included), or a range of lines from the outline. Use it before revising a passage you can't see in full. Each block comes back after its `[#id]`, as in the document section.

heading.description: Heading text of the section to read (case-insensitive, partial match). Takes precedence over the line range.

start_line.description: First line to read, 1-based (as in the outline and search results).

read_file.description: Read a text file, or the text of a PDF, Word, PowerPoint, spreadsheet, EPUB or RTF file (as Markdown), from the project folder, by the relative path find_files or search_files shows. A long file comes back in parts: the answer says which lines of how many it shows and where to read on; pass start_line and end_line to read a part - say, a few dozen lines around a line search_files found.

path.description: Path relative to the project folder

start_line.description: First line to read, 1-based (as in search_files results).

read_file+images.description: Read a text file, or the text of a PDF, Word, PowerPoint, spreadsheet, EPUB or RTF file (as Markdown), from the project folder, by the relative path find_files or search_files shows - or look at an image there (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, up to 6 MB: a map, a photo, a chart, a scanned page). A long file comes back in parts: the answer says which lines of how many it shows and where to read on; pass start_line and end_line to read a part - say, a few dozen lines around a line search_files found.

path.description: Path relative to the project folder

start_line.description: First line to read, 1-based (as in search_files results).

search_conversations.description: Search the user's earlier conversations with you - about every document, newest first - for words, when they refer to something said before that isn't in this conversation or in what you remember ("the title we chose last time", "the names you suggested yesterday"). Every word must be in one message or reply; search for a word or two that would be in it, in the language it was said in. Returns the passages found, with their conversation's title and date.

query.description: A word or two that would be in what was said.

search_document.description: Search the document for a word or phrase (case-insensitive). Returns each matching line with its line number and its block's id, for an edit to name.

query.description: Text to search for in the document

search_files.description: Search every text file and document (PDF, Word, PowerPoint, spreadsheet, EPUB, RTF) in the project folder for a word or phrase (case-insensitive), however long the file. Returns `path:line: text` matches - use it to find where a character, term or fact appears across chapters and notes, then read_file with start_line and end_line around the match for its context.

search_references.description: Search the user's reference library - the papers, books, reports and notes in the project's `{}/` folder - for the passages that best answer a question, ranked by relevance. Pass the words the sources would use; several words are fine and the best passages contain most of them. Each result is `path:first-last` and the passage: cite the source by its file name, and read_file with start_line and end_line for more around it. Prefer it to search_files for research in the references; search_files finds one exact phrase anywhere in the project.

query.description: What the passages should be about, in the sources' own words

use_skill.description: Load the full instructions of one of the available skills (listed in the system prompt), or a reference pack a skill names. Call this before following a skill whenever the user's request matches its description, or when the user invokes it by name.

name.description: The skill's name, exactly as listed, or a reference pack such as standards-fr or standards-fr#dialogue

write_file.description: Create a file in the folder, or replace one's whole text. For a few changes to a file that exists, edit_file is cheaper and safer. Not for the open document - propose_edit changes that. Work across several files: first say in a line or two which files you will change and how, then make the changes without waiting for an answer.

path.description: The file, from the folder, e.g. `chapters/03.md`; folders are made as needed
